#7479. Elon Musk’s Grokipedia is littered with mistakes. But Wikipedia could still learn some things from it.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Grokipedia shows that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet.

When I saw Grokipedia’s articles about me, the memories came rushing back: my 19 years in minor league baseball, including that impressive season with the Montgomery Rebels when I hit 20 home runs. I was lean back then — 6 feet tall and 168 pounds — and earned a career batting average just under .300. I became a minor league coach and managed the Chicago White Sox for a short stint in 1970, which Grokipedia said “highlighted [my] readiness for higher-level responsibilities.”

I then attended Arizona State University, switched to a career in journalism, created the fact-checking site PolitiFact, won a Pulitzer Prize, and now teach journalism at Duke University.

Ah, the memories!…except that I never played minor league baseball, never managed the White Sox, and can only dream about being 6 feet tall. (I’m 5’8″.) Grokipedia, the AI-written encyclopedia of Elon Musk, has confused me with Marion Danne “Bill” Adair, who died in 2002.

That article and another one about “Bill Adair (journalist)” — which really is me — illustrate the many flaws of Grokipedia, which launched a year ago. The articles are littered with mistakes and superfluous details. They are terribly written and ridiculously long. If Grok, the AI engine that wrote this turgid prose, were a student in one of my writing courses, I would give it a D. (Editor’s note: After this article was published, someone updated the inaccurate Grok pages. The original versions are linked here.)

Still, the articles provide valuable lessons for Wikipedia editors who are debating how and when to use AI. Grokipedia adds new content and context that Wikipedia often lacks. It shows that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet and summarizing them in sweeping prose. It can also provide balance to articles that need it.

Grok can’t write worth a lick, but it shows how Wikipedia can take advantage of AI at a time when overworked editors are trying to keep the encyclopedia alive.

Musk launched Grokipedia as an alternative to Wikipedia, which he said was too liberal. (He called it “Wokepedia.”) Still, he trusted it enough to have Grok copy hundreds of thousands of its articles, which is permitted under Wikipedia’s Creative Commons license, and then add content from elsewhere on the internet. With his usual bluster, Musk said his encyclopedia used a new version of his large language model that was good at “cogent analysis.” He said programmers told it to “cycle through the million most popular articles in Wikipedia and add, modify, and delete.” When Grokipedia launched, Musk said he had big aspirations to overtake Wikipedia, which has 68 million articles in more than 300 languages. He said his encyclopedia would be more complete and more balanced and would make smarter use of images and video. Maybe someday. For now, Grokipedia is a massive collection of overly long articles that are often out of date. Its flaws have been well-documented: Articles are littered with mistakes, peddle conspiracy theories, rely on low-credibility sources, and sometimes skew to the right. And although Grokipedia shows edit requests from readers and whether they are approved, the site is not as transparent as Wikipedia, which reveals details about its editors and every change they make. Last spring, Grokipedia mysteriously stopped updating, according to a report by researchers Renée DiResta and Ronald Robertson. It resumed in late September, still a hot mess, but with a more colorful homepage that always seems to feature its article about Musk. Grokipedia has two articles about me: the conflated baseball player one and “Bill Adair (journalist),” the real one, which is incredibly boring, even to me. Both borrow heavily from Wikipedia’s articles about us and enrich them with details found on assorted websites. Wikipedia’s article about me is nicely concise — just 700 words. It is written in the encyclopedia’s signature dry style and doesn’t contain any errors. The article recounts my career, some of the major news events I’ve covered, the two books I’ve written, and the awards I’ve won. But it highlights trivial events from my career, fails to emphasize larger ones, and lacks any criticism of my work. (I have not tried to improve the article because Wikipedia’s conflict of interest policy prohibits people from editing their own bios.) By contrast, Grokipedia’s “Bill Adair (journalist)” is painfully long — 5,600 words. Its greatest value would be to help someone suffering from a sleep disorder. Like a college student trying to meet a word count, Grok stuffed the article with needless details and redundant descriptions. The article tells you about my work with PolitiFact and then tells you again and again. It explains the site’s rating scale eight times and mentions my academic title four times. Despite labels that say “fact-checked by Grok,” both articles had lots of errors. I spotted 32 in the journalist one and so many in the baseball mashup that I couldn’t count them all. Mistakes are not surprising in AI writing, but I discovered interesting patterns that reveal the weaknesses of large language models. In the article about the real me, only seven of the errors were hallucinations in which Grok seemed to create a detail out of thin air. No, I did not win an award from Manhattan College, and no, PolitiFact did not begin by fact-checking the Tampa mayor’s race. Five other errors showed Grok was a lazy researcher that did not look broadly enough to check a claim. Grok said I am the director of Duke’s journalism program, but I left that job five years ago. The sources cited in the article don’t explain Grok’s mistake, so it seems likely it remembered an old announcement and failed to see a newer one that named my successor. The most prevalent errors were in a broad category I’d all cluelessness. These mistakes showed Grok didn’t fully understand what it read, like someone who skimmed an article too quickly. My favorite in this category was when I got credit for a big scoop in 2000 that George W. Bush had a DUI conviction, which the Grokipedia article said had an impact on “late-election discourse.” I wish! Yes, I was among the many journalists who covered that story, but I had no scoop. Together, the errors reveal that Grok is a knucklehead. It doesn’t know what’s important and what’s not. It is simply mashing together details from many web articles about me. Grok only knows what it found on the internet and it lacks experience and perspective to sort out what’s important. The writing is dreadful. The articles read as if Grok was trained on too many online resumes and corporate memos. Grok uses words and phrases like “commenced” and “transitioned” and “multidisciplinary practicum” and “hypotheses on fact-check efficacy.” A typical sentence: “Adair’s approach in this position reflected a commitment to undiluted sourcing and causal analysis of policy impacts, influencing subsequent innovations in political journalism.” Take a close look at that sentence and you’ll see it’s just a mush of buzzwords. I don’t know what “undiluted sourcing” is and have never used the phrase, nor would I refer to “causal analysis”…of anything. Grok is trying to impress us with an MBA vocabulary but is really just an epic bullshitter. Bernadette Meehan, CEO of the Wikimedia Foundation, which provides money and technical infrastructure for the encyclopedia, has called AI “an existential threat” to Wikipedia. The 25-year-old encyclopedia has long been a source and beneficiary of Google searches. Wikipedia provides the answers and in turn benefits from readers clicking through to read articles. But when people make a query to a chatbot, they often get the answer they need in an AI summary and don’t click through to read the encyclopedia article. That threatens donations because fewer readers see Wikipedia’s fundraising pitches. Wikipedia has banned content generated by LLMs, but that hasn’t stopped many contributors — some well-intentioned, some not — from dumping an avalanche of AI-written content on the site. That has put a huge burden on the site’s “New pages patrol,” the editors who approve articles, because they must weed out the lousy content. (Wikipedia has a helpful guide of LLMs’ favorite words and phrases, such as “tapestry” and “meticulously” and sentences that start with “additionally.”) Still, terrible as it is, Grokipedia offers lessons in how AI can help Wikipedia. Grok’s voracious internet searches sometimes find things that human editors don’t. The long article about me includes a substantive discussion of my research about lying in politics and my work with fact-checkers around the world, neither of which are in the Wikipedia version. Grokipedia also provides some welcome balance. When it offers context, Grokipedia can be a little heavy with hype (“His work has been lauded for innovating transparency in media…”) But it also included a “Criticisms and Controversies” section that details complaints that PolitiFact is biased against Republicans. That section has a healthy back and forth about the critiques and my response. That kind of balance could be helpful for Wikipedia, which has taken heat from Musk and others for being too lefty. Musk’s encyclopedia also has a playful spirit that Wikipedia could learn from. Grokipedia’s homepage features random samples of recent edits that provide a glimpse at how the site is being improved. Another Grokipedia feature reads articles aloud in an AI voice you select: Eve, who sounds like a BBC anchor; Ara, a serious woman with crisp diction; Leo, who might have been a professor at Oxford; and Sal, whose name suggests a sports bar but whose voice is NPR. My big takeaway from Grok is the importance of human judgment in curating knowledge. Grok is a bot trying to behave like a human editor. Its many mistakes and lousy writing show that AI is not ready to replace Wikipedia’s talented volunteers. Still, Grok shows that AI can be a tool that helps them research and write better articles. After seeing an AI encyclopedia up close through my experiences with Grok, I come away with hope. Yes, AI can be a sloppy researcher and an awful writer. But Grok’s performance, shaky as it was, highlighted AI’s readiness for higher-level responsibilities. Bill Adair, the Knight Professor of the Practice of Journalism and Public Policy at Duke University, is writing a book about how Wikipedia editors are adapting to the age of AI.

Musk launched Grokipedia as an alternative to Wikipedia, which he said was too liberal. (He called it “Wokepedia.”) Still, he trusted it enough to have Grok copy hundreds of thousands of its articles, which is permitted under Wikipedia’s Creative Commons license, and then add content from elsewhere on the internet.

With his usual bluster, Musk said his encyclopedia used a new version of his large language model that was good at “cogent analysis.” He said programmers told it to “cycle through the million most popular articles in Wikipedia and add, modify, and delete.”

When Grokipedia launched, Musk said he had big aspirations to overtake Wikipedia, which has 68 million articles in more than 300 languages. He said his encyclopedia would be more complete and more balanced and would make smarter use of images and video.

For now, Grokipedia is a massive collection of overly long articles that are often out of date. Its flaws have been well-documented: Articles are littered with mistakes, peddle conspiracy theories, rely on low-credibility sources, and sometimes skew to the right. And although Grokipedia shows edit requests from readers and whether they are approved, the site is not as transparent as Wikipedia, which reveals details about its editors and every change they make.

Last spring, Grokipedia mysteriously stopped updating, according to a report by researchers Renée DiResta and Ronald Robertson. It resumed in late September, still a hot mess, but with a more colorful homepage that always seems to feature its article about Musk.

Grokipedia has two articles about me: the conflated baseball player one and “Bill Adair (journalist),” the real one, which is incredibly boring, even to me. Both borrow heavily from Wikipedia’s articles about us and enrich them with details found on assorted websites. Wikipedia’s article about me is nicely concise — just 700 words. It is written in the encyclopedia’s signature dry style and doesn’t contain any errors. The article recounts my career, some of the major news events I’ve covered, the two books I’ve written, and the awards I’ve won. But it highlights trivial events from my career, fails to emphasize larger ones, and lacks any criticism of my work. (I have not tried to improve the article because Wikipedia’s conflict of interest policy prohibits people from editing their own bios.) By contrast, Grokipedia’s “Bill Adair (journalist)” is painfully long — 5,600 words. Its greatest value would be to help someone suffering from a sleep disorder. Like a college student trying to meet a word count, Grok stuffed the article with needless details and redundant descriptions. The article tells you about my work with PolitiFact and then tells you again and again. It explains the site’s rating scale eight times and mentions my academic title four times. Despite labels that say “fact-checked by Grok,” both articles had lots of errors. I spotted 32 in the journalist one and so many in the baseball mashup that I couldn’t count them all. Mistakes are not surprising in AI writing, but I discovered interesting patterns that reveal the weaknesses of large language models. In the article about the real me, only seven of the errors were hallucinations in which Grok seemed to create a detail out of thin air. No, I did not win an award from Manhattan College, and no, PolitiFact did not begin by fact-checking the Tampa mayor’s race. Five other errors showed Grok was a lazy researcher that did not look broadly enough to check a claim. Grok said I am the director of Duke’s journalism program, but I left that job five years ago. The sources cited in the article don’t explain Grok’s mistake, so it seems likely it remembered an old announcement and failed to see a newer one that named my successor. The most prevalent errors were in a broad category I’d all cluelessness. These mistakes showed Grok didn’t fully understand what it read, like someone who skimmed an article too quickly. My favorite in this category was when I got credit for a big scoop in 2000 that George W. Bush had a DUI conviction, which the Grokipedia article said had an impact on “late-election discourse.” I wish! Yes, I was among the many journalists who covered that story, but I had no scoop. Together, the errors reveal that Grok is a knucklehead. It doesn’t know what’s important and what’s not. It is simply mashing together details from many web articles about me. Grok only knows what it found on the internet and it lacks experience and perspective to sort out what’s important. The writing is dreadful. The articles read as if Grok was trained on too many online resumes and corporate memos. Grok uses words and phrases like “commenced” and “transitioned” and “multidisciplinary practicum” and “hypotheses on fact-check efficacy.” A typical sentence: “Adair’s approach in this position reflected a commitment to undiluted sourcing and causal analysis of policy impacts, influencing subsequent innovations in political journalism.” Take a close look at that sentence and you’ll see it’s just a mush of buzzwords. I don’t know what “undiluted sourcing” is and have never used the phrase, nor would I refer to “causal analysis”…of anything. Grok is trying to impress us with an MBA vocabulary but is really just an epic bullshitter. Bernadette Meehan, CEO of the Wikimedia Foundation, which provides money and technical infrastructure for the encyclopedia, has called AI “an existential threat” to Wikipedia. The 25-year-old encyclopedia has long been a source and beneficiary of Google searches. Wikipedia provides the answers and in turn benefits from readers clicking through to read articles. But when people make a query to a chatbot, they often get the answer they need in an AI summary and don’t click through to read the encyclopedia article. That threatens donations because fewer readers see Wikipedia’s fundraising pitches. Wikipedia has banned content generated by LLMs, but that hasn’t stopped many contributors — some well-intentioned, some not — from dumping an avalanche of AI-written content on the site. That has put a huge burden on the site’s “New pages patrol,” the editors who approve articles, because they must weed out the lousy content. (Wikipedia has a helpful guide of LLMs’ favorite words and phrases, such as “tapestry” and “meticulously” and sentences that start with “additionally.”) Still, terrible as it is, Grokipedia offers lessons in how AI can help Wikipedia. Grok’s voracious internet searches sometimes find things that human editors don’t. The long article about me includes a substantive discussion of my research about lying in politics and my work with fact-checkers around the world, neither of which are in the Wikipedia version. Grokipedia also provides some welcome balance. When it offers context, Grokipedia can be a little heavy with hype (“His work has been lauded for innovating transparency in media…”) But it also included a “Criticisms and Controversies” section that details complaints that PolitiFact is biased against Republicans. That section has a healthy back and forth about the critiques and my response. That kind of balance could be helpful for Wikipedia, which has taken heat from Musk and others for being too lefty. Musk’s encyclopedia also has a playful spirit that Wikipedia could learn from. Grokipedia’s homepage features random samples of recent edits that provide a glimpse at how the site is being improved. Another Grokipedia feature reads articles aloud in an AI voice you select: Eve, who sounds like a BBC anchor; Ara, a serious woman with crisp diction; Leo, who might have been a professor at Oxford; and Sal, whose name suggests a sports bar but whose voice is NPR. My big takeaway from Grok is the importance of human judgment in curating knowledge. Grok is a bot trying to behave like a human editor. Its many mistakes and lousy writing show that AI is not ready to replace Wikipedia’s talented volunteers. Still, Grok shows that AI can be a tool that helps them research and write better articles. After seeing an AI encyclopedia up close through my experiences with Grok, I come away with hope. Yes, AI can be a sloppy researcher and an awful writer. But Grok’s performance, shaky as it was, highlighted AI’s readiness for higher-level responsibilities. Bill Adair, the Knight Professor of the Practice of Journalism and Public Policy at Duke University, is writing a book about how Wikipedia editors are adapting to the age of AI.

#7478. Google Publishes Guidance For Google-Agent Crawler via @sejournal, @martinibuster

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

Google published new guidance for recognizing Google-Agent and allowing its agents to interact with websites securely.

Google published new guidance on how to keep from blocking its user-triggered AI agents that identify themselves as Google-Agent. The new documentation shows how to verify legitimate Google-Agent requests and configure firewalls to allow them on websites.

Google’s new guidance on Google-Agent may be related to its announcement of the expansion of Personal Intelligence, which came after this article was originally published. Both developments are consistent with Google CEO Sundar Pichai’s description of a unified experience across Google’s products and services that’s mediated by an agentic layer.

Personal Intelligence enables Google to draw on information from across its products and services to better understand what users want to accomplish and provide increasingly personalized assistance.

Google’s announcement offers an example of how this works:

“So if you’ve been researching and planning for a trip, you can pick up right where you left off in a new search thread without starting over or repeating yourself.”

Planning a trip can involve researching destinations, comparing accommodations, and making reservations. That’s precisely the kind of task-based search where user-triggered AI agents may fetch information from websites, interact with them, and complete tasks on behalf of users.

What makes the timing of Google’s Google-Agent guidance interesting is that Google is simultaneously expanding its ability to understand what users want to accomplish and publishing guidance for website owners on how to make sure that user-triggered AI agents are not blocked from accessing websites.

Although Google has not explicitly connected Google-Agent to Personal Intelligence, the two developments appear to complement each other in terms of Google’s larger goal of creating a personalized, task-based Search experience.

Google-Agent is the name used by AI agents hosted on Google’s infrastructure that navigate websites and perform actions on behalf of users. Google’s guidance and also Google’s User-Triggered Fetcher documentation do not identify which Google products or services use Google-Agent. Neither documentation mentions Google Search, AI Mode, Gemini, or any other Google product.

It describes Google-Agent as agents that are hosted on Google’s infrastructure, interact with and navigate websites, and complete tasks on behalf of a user.

The document says or implies that the Google-Agent does the following:

The new guidance explains there are three ways that website owners can verify that a request comes from Google-Agent.

1. The request’s User-Agent header contains “Google-Agent.”

2. The request originates from an IP address listed in Google’s published file of user-triggered agent ranges.

3. Only where it’s present, when the request carries a cryptographic signature under Google’s experimental Web Bot Auth protocol, which can be checked against Google’s published public keys.

The first two checks are the baseline, and the signature check adds stronger verification when it’s available. A Google-Agent bot can then be allowed through whatever bot defenses are in use once it passes those checks. Google also notes that some CDNs and bot-detection services handle this verification automatically.

Lastly, Google offers guidance on troubleshooting when the Google-Agent is unintentionally blocked.

Google recommends ensuring that rules allowing Google-Agent requests have higher priority and are evaluated before broader blocking rules, including:

If bot detection, firewall (WAF), or CDN rules only covers the initial page request, the agent will be able to land on the website but it will be unable to finish whatever task it’s there to accomplish.

Google recommends checking that CAPTCHA challenges are disabled for verified Google-Agent requests, reviewing rate limits, IP address updates, and proxy configurations.

“Proxy headers: Confirm that load balancers and intermediate proxies preserve the original client IP, the User-Agent header, and (for signed requests) the Signature, Signature-Input, and Signature-Agent headers.”

Google’s new guidance addresses three issues to check if Google-Agent is being inadvertently blocked:

“Shared-IP rate limits: Confirm that per-IP rate-limiting rules account for or exempt verified Google-Agent IP ranges, as concurrent requests from multiple users share the same egress pool.

IP range updates: Confirm that IP-based rules stay synced with the latest ranges in user-triggered-agents.json.

Proxy headers: Confirm that load balancers and intermediate proxies preserve the original client IP, the User-Agent header, and (for signed requests) the Signature, Signature-Input, and Signature-Agent headers.”

Google’s new Google-Agent guidance offers tips for website owners who want to allow Google-Agent interactions, stressing that they need to make sure that legitimate Google-Agent requests can pass through security defenses without compromising protections against unwanted bots.

#7477. Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft will make it easier for publishers to opt out of being scraped

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Right now, if you don’t want your site to be scraped by AI companies, you have to block each company’s crawlers individually. On Friday, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft said they would support a common robots.txt signal that, per OpenAI, “makes it easier for publishers and website operators to communicate the same preference to multiple participating providers at once.”

Anthropic engineer Kevin Kelley proposed the common signal as part of work for the Internet Engineering Task Force, and Anthropic is already supporting it. OpenAI says it will do so “in the coming months,” and Google and Microsoft say they’ll do so next year.

Meta VP of communications Andy Stone called the common signal “an important step,” writing in a tweet that the company supports “publishers’ ability to express preferences about how their content is used for foundational generative AI training.” Meta is under scrutiny for proposed commercial terms that would allow broad scraping; last week, it agreed to delay implementation of those terms.

A few other highlights from the earnings:

Let me just start by saying, we’ve got really big ambitions in video for The Times to be as preferred a brand to watch as it is to read and listen. This is a kind of long bet that we can grow engagement from the audience we have, and also grow audience, because we’re going to engage new people in different ways. I’m not sure what you’re referring to operationally. We’ve been in a sort of steady state of scaling production in the newsroom of video, and that’s happening in myriad ways. We also continue to have a big effort on visual investigations, which we’ve referred to in prior quarters and in prepared remarks. We’ve got another one coming from one of the hosts of The Daily. #7473. Partner Solutions Architect , AI Builder at Supabase

Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

Supabase is the backend of choice for a growing wave of AI-native builders, and we're deepening structured partnerships with the platforms they build on top of — Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable. These partners' teams are talking to thousands of developers and agents who need exactly what we build—a full backend platform with Postgres at the core—without the vendor lock-in. This is an opportunity to get Supabase in front of the right partner SAs and make us the default recommendation for a modern, AI-ready backend.

We’re looking for a Platform Solutions Architect to join our Success Team and help embed Supabase into the Solutions and Engineering communities with AI Builders.

You’ll work closely with Partner Solutions Architects and Partner Engineers at Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable, helping us proactively identify builder problems where Supabase is the right solution and closing the gap between partner intent and real developer outcomes. This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions of AI-native apps and agents.

In this role, you’ll focus on three core pillars:

Build deep relationships with Technical counterparts at Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable, focusing initially on defined use cases and agent/app-migration motions.

Develop and deliver technical workshops, training materials, and enablement content to give partner SAs the fluency to position Supabase.

Create demos, integration guides, and reference architectures that make Supabase’s fit with Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable immediately legible.

Partner with SAs at these companies on active opportunities to move deals forward and feeding technical pipeline intelligence back to the alliance lead.

Resolve blockers for partner SAs working on Supabase implementations to maintain their credibility with the builders they support.

Troubleshoot complex integration scenarios and turn solutions into reusable assets.

Maintain a close feedback loop with Supabase product and engineering teams to ensure technical guidance reflects the latest platform capabilities.

Measure success through co-sell opportunities sourced, influenced deals, and SA enablement metrics across the Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable partnerships.

Write technical blog posts and case studies that demonstrate real-world Supabase implementations built on Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable.

Represent Supabase at conferences, meetups, and partner-sponsored events (e.g. Anthropic and OpenAI dev days, Vercel Ship, Lovable community events).

Develop video content and interactive learning experiences to reduce the "time-to-fluency" for partner SAs.

Have 5+ years of experience in technical roles with deep hands-on experience building on modern AI infrastructure. Previous experience working at Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, Lovable (or a similar AI builder platform) or as a partner to one is required.

Understand how partner SAs at AI builder platforms are incentivized, how they make recommendations, and how the partner ecosystem influences developer decisions.

Communicate clearly across both technical and non-technical audiences, explaining complex concepts with ease.

Have a strong technical foundation in PostgreSQL, APIs, and modern development frameworks like React and Next.js, plus fluency with AI/agent tooling (LLM APIs, MCP, agent frameworks).

Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and moving quickly to build a playbook from scratch.

Are energized by solving real-world problems for developers building the next generation of AI-native products.

We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

Once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

#7472. The Final Ad Checklist Before BFCM – What To Fix Now & What To Leave via @sejournal, @tonyadam

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

Keep Black Friday ads running with final checks on Google budget limits, Meta spend caps, purchase tracking, and offer consistency before Cyber Monday.

Your Black Friday advertising should now be built, paced, and approved. The useful work left is checking what’s running will continue running and being honest about anything that isn’t ready. Some of it can still be fixed in the few days before Black Friday on Nov. 27, and some of it belongs on next year’s plan.

This is the checklist our team works through on the accounts we run through the end of the holiday season. Most of this is dull stuff, sure, but the last thing you want is something like this breaking at the worst possible time. So think of it like our checklist being passed on to you to make sure that doesn’t happen.

If you have not built campaigns by now, you are really cutting it close and leaving it for last minute. For the accounts we run, the freeze date was last Friday, Nov. 20, and since then the only changes going in are fixes or tweaks. Any major changes now could trigger you right back into learning mode, and you don’t want that. Campaigns should be structured, stable, and running leading into Black Friday Cyber Monday (BFCM).

If something still isn’t built, only launch low-risk pieces, like a brand campaign if you somehow don’t have one, or promo creative inside an asset group or ad set that already has history. Anything structural goes on next year’s plan.

Pacing should have started in early November, so budgets are already close to where you want them on Black Friday instead of sitting at an October level waiting for one big jump on Thursday. Frankly speaking, most companies start their BFCM offers early, so if that’s you, you have nothing to worry about here because you might already be ramped up.

On Meta, the ramp should have happened in steps, since frequent budget changes can send ad sets back into learning. Meta’s developer documentation describes budget scheduling as a way to “schedule budget increases for your campaign or ad set budget” for days when you expect higher sales. If you scheduled increases, check the dates and amounts against your sale.

On Google, a campaign can spend up to twice its average daily budget on a given day, and no more than 30.4 times the average daily budget over the month. When you change a budget partway through the month, Google recalculates the monthly limit as what you’ve spent so far plus the new daily budget times the remaining calendar days, counting the day of the edit.

Cyber Monday 2026 falls on Nov. 30, the last day of the month, so if you raise a budget that morning, the monthly limit becomes what you’ve spent plus one day of the new budget, and you won’t be charged for more than that one day regardless of the 2x daily allowance. A campaign that runs close to double its budget Friday through Sunday is also using the monthly room Cyber Monday would have had. So treat Black Friday through Cyber Monday as one stretch, set those budgets before the weekend, and check on Sunday night how much monthly room your key campaigns have left.

Google’s campaign total budgets let you set one budget for a three- to 90-day window on Performance Max, Search, and Shopping, but they’re only available for new campaigns, so this isn’t the week to start using them. The monthly limit starts over on Dec. 1, so set December budgets now as well.

If budgets haven’t ramped, raise Google budgets today, since the change takes effect immediately and the rest of the month paces to the new number. On Meta, start stepping budgets up today rather than all at once on Thursday night. And write down the budget you wish you’d had on November 1, because that’s where next year’s ramp starts.

See also: Google Ads Channel Priorities Have Limits – What PMax Still Won’t Let You Split

A few things can’t be checked in a settings screen, so these are the questions I’d want an honest answer to before Thursday, and what I’d do if the answer is no.

Prospecting funded in September and October is what pays during BFCM. In our accounts, upper-funnel spend takes roughly six to eight weeks to show up in revenue, which is why I argued that September was the last month to fund it. Your own lag depends on price point and how long people take to decide.

If the answer is no: Don’t launch cold prospecting this week, when in our accounts prospecting CPMs are at their highest of the year. Keep the prospecting you have on a flat budget through the week and let harvest campaigns take the extra money. Put the build on next year’s calendar for September, as a fixed budget rather than a percentage of whatever is left.

It should lean towards Bottom Of Funnel (BoFu). BFCM is when the demand you built in the fall turns into orders, so retargeting, brand search, and your existing customers are going to take a bigger share of spend than they do the rest of the year. During the holidays, those sales are worth buying. What matters is that it was a decision. Before the week starts, you should know roughly how much budget is going to people who already know you, how much stays on new customers, and what the floor is for prospecting so it doesn’t get raided the first time retargeting looks great on Friday morning.

Keep in mind that during BFCM, your email, SMS, retargeting, and brand campaigns are often all reaching the same person for the same order, and each one will report it. So don’t move budget into retargeting just because its ROAS looks great on Black Friday. Check it against what the store is actually doing overall before you add more.

You can see the split on both platforms. On Google, lifecycle goal reporting adds a “New vs. returning customers” segment to the Campaigns table on campaigns where the new customer acquisition goal is turned on, and on Meta, audience segments break sales campaign results into new, engaged, and existing customers once you’ve defined them in your ad account settings.

If the answer is no: Decide it today. Write down the prospecting floor and the rough share for new versus existing customers through Cyber Monday, and look at the new versus returning numbers each morning so you’re adjusting against the plan instead of against whichever campaign has the best ROAS that day.

You should by now. Testing is what October is for, and BFCM is when you have winning creative you know you can put advertising dollars against. That matters most on Meta, where the creative is doing most of the targeting in Advantage+, so in our accounts, a proven concept with the offer added to it tends to beat a brand new idea during holiday shopping. The offer can go on as an overlay, in the first few seconds of a video, or in the headline, without changing what made the ad work in the first place.

If the answer is no: Look back at the last 60 to 90 days, pick the best performer on each platform by cost per purchase, and add the offer to that. Don’t run a creative test during the most expensive week of the year, because whatever wins under BFCM pricing won’t tell you much about January. Put an October testing window on next year’s plan, so you go into the holiday season with your winners already picked.

Every date through December should have creative approved and paused: Black Friday, Cyber Monday, any Cyber Week extension, shipping deadlines, last-minute gifts and gift cards, and post-Christmas on Dec. 26.

Google’s ad review page says most ads are reviewed within one business day and “changes to your ad or assets restart the review process and may cause delays.” Meta’s Marketing API best practices say changes to creative or targeting trigger review and that an ad entering review while paused stays paused after approval.

If the answer is no: Submit what’s missing today with final copy and schedule it with end dates, because Thanksgiving week is short on business days and a typo caught after approval means another trip through review.

Place a real order with your promo code and follow it into Google Ads and Meta Events Manager. A tag check only confirms that something fired, and a checkout change made in November can alter the value your purchase event sends without stopping it from firing.

If something is off, it’s worth pulling a developer in before Wednesday. If tracking breaks during the week anyway, fix it and apply a data exclusion so the bidder doesn’t learn from the broken days. Cancel the test order afterward.

The site banner, landing page, sale price in your feed, Merchant Center promotions, and ad copy should all say the same thing, because a mismatch usually shows up as disapprovals the morning the sale starts. Merchant Center’s automatic item updates are on by default and correct prices from your landing pages, but Google says they may not work for products whose price changes more than once a day.

Push your own feed updates for any hourly doorbusters, run a purchase on the promo landing page from a phone the way a customer would, and name the person who opens Merchant Center diagnostics first thing Black Friday.

Billing is the item most likely to stop every ad you have. Google says a declined payment can stop the account, and on monthly invoicing, once costs reach the account budget, “all ads in the account stop running.” On Meta, the ad account spend cap is a hard stop, and “when the amount is reached, all delivery stops.”

Raise the invoiced account budget to cover the higher spend through Nov. 30, reset any Meta spend cap, check the card on file, and give at least two people admin access on both platforms and Merchant Center, with two-step verification on devices they’ll have over the holiday.

Several Google Ads features that add promotions or pick landing pages are on by default, so go through them before your own promotion goes live.

I wouldn’t switch all of this off on principle. Decide on each one during the holidays and note what you changed so you can revisit it in January.

Your brand campaign should be fully funded through Cyber Monday, and even into December. Keep an eye on auction insights daily to see which competitors are bidding on your brand. I know I’m stating the obvious, but this is definitely not the time of the year to let a competitor steal a brand sale. Be defensive, buy your brand terms, and keep that impression share % high. Keeping brand in its own campaign, which I’ve argued for before, makes a “Limited By Budget” status obvious the morning it happens.

On one premium brand we work with, several competitors were bidding on the brand name, and we’ve consistently managed brand spend throughout the year, but during holiday shopping times, we max out impression share %.

Once the checks are done, the hardest part of Black Friday advertising is leaving the account alone and letting it run. Of course, make sure there is someone keeping an eye on it from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday and have a plan in place for what can change. Does pacing increase at all? If so, what % increase is the cap? Should any creative be swapped out? Messaging?

We keep that checklist pretty short: budgets on campaigns that are hitting target and fixes for tracking or disapprovals, and everything else waits until Dec. 1.

Keep a running list throughout the week of anything you couldn’t fix, whether that’s prospecting you never built, creative you didn’t get to test, or the budget you wish you’d started with in early November. It’s the most useful thing you’ll have when you start planning next year’s holiday season, and it’s a lot easier to write down this week than to piece together in January, or even next year.

Check that budgets have ramped, that tracking records the right value on a real promo order, that billing won’t stop your ads, and that your offer matches across site, feed, and ads. Campaigns and creative should already be built, so the week is for checks and fixes.

Enough that your best campaigns aren’t capped on Black Friday or Cyber Monday, based on your own past results rather than a round number. With Cyber Monday on November 30, set Google budgets before the weekend, since a budget raised on the last day of the month only gets one day of room.

For this year, mostly yes. In our accounts, upper-funnel spend takes roughly six to eight weeks to show up in revenue, so prospecting launched now is bought at peak prices and mostly pays out in January. Keep what you have running and plan next year’s build for September.

No. Results from BFCM week don’t carry over well to the rest of the year, and an untested concept is an expensive bet at peak prices. Put the offer on proven creative and test in October.

Yes. If competitors bid on your brand and you don’t, you can lose those sales to them. Keep brand in its own campaign with enough budget and check auction insights daily through Cyber Week.

#7470. Weird animals win on Instagram. Mongabay’s next-best choice? Its reporters.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories.’”

Mongabay’s most successful videos are about weird animals.

But not every video from the environmental newsroom can be about strange — or strangely cute — animals. Some have to be about shrimp farm pollution. Or a deforestation crisis brought on by cacao farming in Liberia. That’s where the challenge comes in, Mongabay video managing editor Lucia Torres has found. Turning that kind of journalism into something people stop scrolling for isn’t easy.

“Generally mass audiences are less interested in environmental content on YouTube [and] Instagram,” Torres said. “We have to compete with recipes, music videos, etc.”

Mongabay publishes around 150 to 200 videos a year with a team of four full-time and one half-time producers. These include short vertical videos on YouTube Shorts and Instagram; evergreen explainers around “complex enviro-problems”; twice-monthly features; and lengthy investigations or short documentaries.

To reach new audiences with its environmental journalism, Mongabay started experimenting with behind-the-scenes reels in late 2024. At the time, Mongabay’s Instagram reels averaged 2,000 to 3,000 views. Torres said she was inspired by behind-the-scenes videos from National Geographic, The New York Times, ProPublica, and contributing creator Izzy Sasada. An early behind-the-scenes video — on pollution from those shrimp farms — drew about 14,000 views. Additional videos from California and Indonesia each got about 6,000 views. Mongabay started to dive deeper with videos that featured sources and reporters filming from the field.

A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay)

From the initial tests, it became clear to Torres that the best-performing videos were ones with behind-the-scenes footage from investigations or collaborations. Putting reporters on camera — in the field or at their desks — worked.

“The content [on platforms like Instagram] is dominated now by individual content creators,” said Torres, who is currently a Knight Science Journalism Fellow at MIT. She said Mongabay is “still figuring out how we can create personalities or creators within the organization that represent what Mongabay does — that are good journalists but also good at talking in front of the camera.”

A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay)

Another successful example came with Mongabay’s investigation into vanishing forests in Liberia. The piece ran as a long-form article, a lengthy YouTube video, and a behind-the-scenes short.

A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay)

Mongabay now plans its multimedia packages for big investigative stories from the beginning. “They require cross-team, high-level collaborations,” Torres said. “You really have to think about all the elements you are going to use before starting production so when you’re in the field you get everything you need.”

Not everything has panned out. Last year, Mongabay tried a data visualization series on climate data. It didn’t work. The lessons for the newsroom went beyond video.

“People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories,’” Torres said. “The simple mention of ‘climate’ scares them away.”

CEO and founder Rhett Butler has seen the same thing across Mongabay’s journalism.

“We’re seeing strong evidence that doomer stories are resonating less with our audiences,” he said. “Climate stories — especially those focused on disasters or the climate emergency — tend to garner less interest than other topics.” The ones that do well, he added, have “an ecosystem or wildlife angle, give readers a sense of agency, or present a solution.”

Mongabay has responded by introducing more projects and series focused on solutions journalism, like Indigenous-led conservation, agroecology, and conservation technology.

RELATED ARTICLEAudience editors offer advice for “dispiriting” times in social and searchSarah ScireJanuary 16, 2025“We’ve also been sharing data with the newsroom about which kinds of framing are reaching more people right now, so writers and editors can consider whether they might want to incorporate how people are responding to problems into their stories,” Butler said. “But we aren’t overly prescriptive, so ultimately it’s up to editors and writers how they use this information.”

Looking at the 3,422 articles published between June 1, 2025 and August 31, 2026, Butler found that the median story featuring hope or a solution got 41% more traffic than articles that only described the crisis or threat. (Articles classified as being about an “action confronting a threat” got 43% more.)

Today, 71% of the 100 most-read stories on Mongabay’s English-language site can be classified as “hope / solution / agency” or “action confronting a threat,” Butler said. Only 21% were “doom only.”

The video team has done something similar. The environmental newsroom’s short series Stranger Creatures leads with “the wonder of wild creatures first,” Torres noted. The conservation or endangered species angle follows.

“We’ve stopped framing stories as a climate problem, and started framing stories from a solutions-oriented, action-driven perspective, community-first, or fun-stuff first,” Torres said. “Climate is implicit now in the stories.”

What video won’t be, at least for now, is a revenue generator. Almost all of Mongabay’s revenue comes from contributions and grants, according to its annual report. (Events, licensing, and advertising “are insignificant at this point,” Butler said.)

“I’m not bullish on video becoming a material source of revenue for Mongabay, given how the space has evolved and our position in it,” Butler said. “Ten years ago I was a lot more optimistic on that front.”

Part of the problem, he said, is incentives. “Building a video strategy around advertising creates an incentive to prioritize views, which may not align with our broader organizational emphasis on impact,” Butler said. “The stories that attract the largest audiences aren’t necessarily those most likely to inform decisions or prompt action.”

#7467. The Onion’s new plan to market its print newspaper: sponsoring a bowl game

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

College football already has an Orange Bowl, a Peach Bowl, and a Citrus Bowl, so on its face, there’s nothing outlandish about the concept of an Onion Bowl.

But this matchup wouldn’t be titled to evoke some locale’s bumper crop, à la the Famous Idaho Potato Bowl. Instead it would market “America’s Finest News Source,” The Onion. (Today’s top headlines: Bain Capital Acquires Tibetan Buddhism For $35 Million; Abdul El-Sayed Makes History As First Physically Healthy Senator; Chuck Schumer Delivers Victory Speech To Previously Enthusiastic Crowd.)

On Thursday morning, Onion CEO (and past Nieman Lab contributor) Ben Collins announced the publication’s quest to buy naming rights for a bowl game, both on Bluesky and on the podcast Pablo Torre Finds Out:

The Onion is extremely close to buying an honest-to-goodness, Division 1 college football bowl series bowl game.

Yes, we're trying to pull off The Onion Bowl.

A few days before Christmas, potentially in Texas.

But we've already been banned once. And we need your help.

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:32 AM

For those unfamiliar, American college football seasons traditionally end with a few dozen bowl games, scattered around the country (and occasionally outside it). Nearly all of these games sell naming rights to one company or another, leading to fun combinations like the Poulan Weed Eater Independence Bowl, the TaxSlayer.com Gator Bowl, and the Union Home Mortgage Gasparilla Bowl. Collins wants to buy the rights to one of the several bowl games that are still without a sponsor for their games next month.

This absurdity — though no more absurd, I suppose, than the Snoop Dogg Arizona Bowl presented by Gin & Juice by Dre and Snoop — serves as the excellent marketing hook to get people to buy a $75/year print subscription, a major driver of The Onion’s revenue.

Indeed, only three U.S. newspapers have a daily print circulation over 100,000 — The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, and the New York Post; The Washington Post and USA Today have already fallen below that line. (At the risk of being pedantic, though, The Onion appears in print monthly, not daily, making it a bit of an apples-to-oranges comparison. Also, The Onion gets to make up its stories.)

Collins says The Onion actually got quite close to buying the naming rights to the New Orleans Bowl, which last year lost its longtime naming sponsor, the…Ohio-based freight-shipping concern R+L Carriers? The Onion was prepared to pay “mid six figures.” But the organization that runs the bowl, the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation, apparently said no deep into the process, a move Collins attributed to “politics.” (I reached out to the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation for comment — a sentence I did not expect to type today — but did not hear back.)

So the guys who sell bowl games ushered us to what we thought was a pretty good fit: The New Orleans Bowl.

I love New Orleans. I love having crawfish out of the back of a pickup truck at 3 a.m. The game would've been in the Superdome two days before Christmas. Good fit! Right? Right???

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:38 AM

Then the folks who run the New Orleans Bowl, a commission that includes representatives of the city and state of Louisiana, found out our plans to highlight our mascot:

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:39 AM

Despite getting all approvals from ESPN and scraping together the cash, right as we were about to sign the paper work to put The Onion Sports Bowl in New Orleans, their state-funded commission called us and said it straight up: "No."

We asked why. They said politics. And the Sickos Guy.

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:40 AM

While the New Orleans Bowl might be out, several currently-brand-free possibilities remain, including the Frisco Bowl in newly blue Texas — the state also home to The Onion’s rival to the death, Alex Jones.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

Google says the back button hijacking policy applies to visits from social media and other channels, and that sites can keep using ad platform code.

Google’s back button hijacking policy applies whenever the hijacking happens in a browser, including on visits from social media rather than Google Search, according to an FAQ Google added to its spam policies today.

Ad platform code is still allowed, the FAQ says, and Google acts only on pages that show the hijacking.

Google’s Search Central changelog says the FAQ answers common questions it has received about the policy. I covered the policy when Google announced it in April, with enforcement set to start June 15.

One FAQ question asks whether the back button hijacking policy covers people who arrive from a non-Search channel, such as social media, and then can’t get back to where they came from. Google wrote:

“If back button hijacking happens when a user is browsing within a browser, then the policy applies.”

A separate answer says “Discover is a part of Google Search and our spam policies apply to Discover as well.” That answer covers Google’s spam policies in general, not only this one.

For a website that opens an external app, which then keeps the user from getting back to the site, the FAQ says “app navigation and ‘open in app’ behaviors are outside the scope of the back button hijacking policy.”

Google’s FAQ shows how the policy applies to visits in a browser and where external app navigation falls outside its scope.

Google’s April announcement said some back button hijacking “may originate from the site’s included libraries or advertising platform,” and asked sites to remove or turn off the code behind it.

The FAQ asks whether Google is preventing sites from importing code hosted by advertising platforms. Google wrote:

“No, site owners can continue to work with advertising platforms and import code that they host. We only take action on pages that exhibit back button hijacking behavior.”

A back button test that starts from a Google results page doesn’t cover every visit the hijacking policy applies to. Test pages that carry ad code by arriving from a social media link and pressing back, and repeat it from Discover when one of your pages shows up there.

Google’s answer on ad code lets you keep your ad partners. The thing to remove is the code or setting on a page that interferes with the back button, wherever it comes from.

Google’s FAQ also says users can report back button hijacking through its spam report form. Those reports go toward improving Google’s spam detection systems, which gives people who hit hijacking on a social or Discover visit a way to flag a site.

#7464. With “Bimbo University,” Nikita Redkar leans into femininity to explain the news

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

“I’m the person who’s holding the door open and being like, ‘OK, you just got here, this is what we’re talking about right now.’”

The data is in: News creators and influencers are a major source of news for Americans, especially people under 30. This is the latest edition of Creators of Record, an occasional series of interviews with popular creators about how they do their jobs.

For Nikita Redkar, a big part of filming a video is putting together an outfit.

In a July video about youth-led protests in India, the 33-year-old is walking around New York City explaining how movements grow when people with opposing views come together on the things they do agree on. She’s wearing a white tube top and black jeans with sunglasses holding her hair back, along with a matching gold necklace and earrings that look like soda can tabs. You can’t see her shoes, but they clack enough for you to know she’s wearing a heel.

In another about comedian Shane Gillis’s Saturday Night Live monologue in which he called women “whores” for wearing shorts to the gym, she’s seated on the floor of her living room wearing a black silk velvet top with a pink faux-fur collar and sleeve cuffs. In the style of a Get Ready With Me video, she explains how 2000s comedy and pop culture entrenched misogynistic ideas of gender roles while applying her makeup.

A full-time news creator who mostly focuses on American politics and culture through a leftist and feminist lens, Redkar calls herself a “professor at Bimbo University.” The girliness is the point, she told me.

“I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice these parts of yourself to be taken seriously,” Redkar said. “You should be taken seriously no matter what.”

Redkar and I chatted in October about how she does her job, leaning into her femininity to explain the news, and what her relationship with social media is like. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Hanaa’ Tameez: How did you start creating news videos? Nikita Redkar: I started in 2022, kind of accidentally. I did standup comedy for five years before the pandemic. I was always doing political humor. I took many political science classes in college, I wrote for the college newspaper, and I always had an interest in politics. In 2022, I had a video that really took off — like millions of views within a few hours. I was explaining the Russian invasion of Ukraine with a silly metaphor about Russia being a jealous ex that doesn’t want to see his ex thrive and be independent. I tried that formula again a couple weeks later…about NATO and fears of World War III. I explained exactly what would be affected. I said there’s not going to be a world war, but things are going to get really expensive, which happened. I also used a girly friendship metaphor for that video. That’s when I started doing that formula — leaning into hyper-femininity to explain these complex geopolitical topics.

Tameez: Tell me about why this work is important to you. Redkar: I feel like my work has made a lot of these daunting topics a little bit more accessible. I incorporate a lot of humor, which is important because there’s a lot of doom and gloom on social media. It’s a normal reaction to have toward everything that’s going on, and I feel it myself, too. But when I talk to my audience, I intentionally give them hope. I don’t just tell the news, but tell them, OK, if we really locked in and held these corporations and the government accountable and we were intentional in our activism, this is what the world could look like. It’s important to make information accessible because we are going through so much news-wise and not all of it is easy to understand. I enjoy bringing this information I’m naturally interested in to people in a way where everyone [can] get involved. When I was starting, I was not [a stereotypical] history buff or a news junkie. I would like to think that someone who looks like me and talks like me should be just as interested in politics and just as interested in the outcome of this country.

When I was starting, I was not [a stereotypical] history buff or a news junkie. I would like to think that someone who looks like me and talks like me should be just as interested in politics and just as interested in the outcome of this country.

Tameez: Tell me more about that. You have a little bit of an online persona. Redkar: That was the whole reason I created Bimbo University. I wanted to get more women on board with being interested in politics and history in particular, because history is seen as such a male-dominated [field]. It was really important to me to bring, colloquially speaking, the girls and the gays and the theys into the space, because it is fascinating and it provides context to what we’re going through right now. It makes the present a little less daunting when you study historical cycles and realize that people 100 years ago dealt with [similar things to what we’re going through now]. How did they come out of that?

How did they come out of that?

Tameez: How do you define your niche and how did you get there? Redkar: My niche is educational. Bimbo University is a place where anyone can start no matter where they are [in their political education]. My audience [ranges from] people who are just getting into politics to people who maybe were triggered by a specific event in the news to start paying more attention to it. I feel like leftist content creators all operate on a spectrum. You have people who are getting really deep into Marxist theory, for example, and things like geopolitics. I’m at the beginning. I’m the person who’s holding the door open and being like, “OK, you just got here, this is what we’re talking about right now.”

Tameez: You’re the first news creator I’ve talked to who does Get Ready With Me videos. You take all of your interests and apply them [to your videos] to be relatable. Redkar: I got into this huge argument with my best friend’s mom, who was a second-wave feminist in the 70s and 80s. She was upset that I called my page Bimbo University. She was like, “You’re dumbing yourself down. Women shouldn’t dumb themselves down. You are just as smart as a man, if not smarter than a man.” That was my lightbulb moment of, oh, your feminism has always been to measure your worth as equal to a man and by the standards of men…working toward a man’s acceptance. In some industries, you’ve got to do that. I don’t blame [people] for thinking like that. But the reason I dial so deep into this hyper-femininity — leaning into these girly things like getting ready with me or walking with my outfit showing — is because I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice those parts of yourself to be taken seriously. You should be taken seriously no matter what.

But the reason I dial so deep into this hyper-femininity — leaning into these girly things like getting ready with me or walking with my outfit showing — is because I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice those parts of yourself to be taken seriously. You should be taken seriously no matter what.

A post shared by Nikita Redkar (@nikitadumptruck)

Redkar: On Mondays, I have a researcher and we go through the topics that people are talking about on social media. We pull up some news sites and see what the big stories are, and we leave some room for breaking news throughout the week.

My week is [split] between videos [on topics] that the general public is talking about, and videos that are just interesting to me. That’s how I stay sane in this business. I’m lucky to have the flexibility of doing that. My researcher combs through news sites and research papers and compiles all that information for me, then I put together a script.

Redkar: It’s definitely my favorite color, but it’s like the chicken and the egg — I don’t know if I liked it before I was doing this.

I pick whatever outfit I feel cute in. In getting ready with me videos, I start with a completely bare face, so at least the outfit has to be giving a little bit.

Tameez: Tell me about the Get Ready with Me videos. How do you decide what’s a GRWM and what’s a walking video?

Redkar: It’s like: What am I comfortable screaming out in the streets versus what do I need to keep at home? Some topics require more seriousness; if it does, I can do the GRWM for that. But if it’s something [less serious], I can be walking my dog or have on some ridiculous outfit.

Redkar: If I get a fact wrong, I’ll do a follow-up video. It’s rare that I’ve gotten a fact wrong because between me and my researcher, that’s two levels of checks before something hits the internet.

For one video, I didn’t factually get it wrong, but I should have included more of the story. It was about the Ugandan dictator Idi Amin and how Indians were expelled from Uganda, which is kind of how we got both Zohran Mamdani and Charli XCX [living in the U.S.], because both of their parents were part of the group that was expelled. I disregarded the racism that local Ugandans faced because of the Indians. I just focused on the expulsion and I framed Indians as the victims.

A lot of people in the comments were like, “Hey, like, you really should have said this other part too.” I just deleted that video, because I didn’t want this to spread and only give half of the story.

Redkar: My favorite video in recent memory was about girls on the first date, how we’re all so vigilant these days about dating men. I had so much fun doing it because I was talking about how life is affected by politics, instead of just politics. I think that video did really well because a lot of people connected to it.

Last year I did a video that I called “How we went from Brat Summer to Hitler Winter” and talked about the hedonism of the 2024 summer and the fascism that followed. I related it to the Roaring 20s transitioning to the Great Depression to the World War. I incorporated a lot of pop culture [references].

A post shared by Nikita Redkar (@nikitadumptruck)

Redkar: Constantly. I posted a video about the Cornell professor who invented the term sexual harassment. I thought it was so interesting and timely, but it did not do well at all. The problem with content creation is sometimes you can’t tell if people didn’t like a video or if you’re being shadow banned.

Redkar: I really love Liz Plank. She’s @feministabulous on Instagram. I love her coverage and how she leans into current conversations in pop culture.

I really like Charles McBryde. He’s not talking about just news — he’s very foreign policy-focused as well.

@MissEatingGood on Instagram is a great explainer of what’s going on and the historical context.

Redkar: Just finding ways to work together. I think there is so much benefit in that. I know countless creators who take a journalist’s article and dissect it down. Maybe [the journalists] should be the ones doing that.

I would happily pair up with journalists and teach them the ins and outs of content creation and how to make a short-form video article that’s also attention-grabbing. That’s just the reality; people are on social media, everyone’s attention span is shot, which sucks. We could try to fix that, but at this moment, we’re not fixing it. It’s really helpful to go on social media and talk [about your reporting] because journalists work hard on their articles.

Creators [should] take more time. We rush way too much. It’s not our fault, because these platforms reward you for making content more frequently and punish you if you take a few days off. [Not rushing] sucks, but what can you do? It’s better than putting incorrect, or rushed, or incomplete information out there.

#7463. Senior Product Designer, Developer Platform at LiveKit

LiveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the voice-driven era of computing. Our platform gives developers everything they need to build, test, deploy, scale, and observe agents in production. Founded in 2021, LiveKit powers voice AI applications for OpenAI, xAI, Salesforce, Coursera, Spotify, and thousands of others, collectively facilitating billions of calls each year.

Most product designers want to design for everyone. This role is for someone who'd rather design for one very specific, very opinionated person: the developer at 2am trying to figure out why their voice agent just failed a call. You'll design the tools developers use to test, evaluate and debug AI agents — a category that's still being invented, with no established patterns to copy. If dense data, real-time systems and reading a stack trace sound more fun than intimidating, keep reading.

You'll thrive as a Senior Product Designer if you:

are obsessed with making the best product for our customers

are known as the go-to person for tackling tough problems

are focused on polish, detail and quality

are a fast learner, frequently picking up new tips, tricks, and skills

The best way to impress us is with thoughtful ways you'd implement LiveKit, and potentially tinkering with it 😊

Own the design of how developers test, evaluate and observe their agents — simulations, evals, logs and agent insights

Turn complex, real-time data into interfaces that are easy to scan, understand and act on

Design new interaction patterns for AI-native workflows, where agents generate the first draft and humans adjust it

Prototype in code and work hand-in-hand with engineers to ship polished work

Contribute patterns to our design system for dense, debugging-oriented surfaces

You've shipped design work for developer tools, observability or data-heavy products

You have strong data-visualization instincts and know when a chart beats a table (and when it doesn't)

You're comfortable in code — reading PRs, tweaking Tailwind, building prototypes

You earn the trust of deeply technical users and engineers

Experience designing for AI or agent tooling

AI tools are already a core part of how you design

An opportunity to build something truly impactful to the world

Contribute to open source alongside world-class engineers
